item.title: Canada, India closer to new economic pact following trade talks in New Delhi, Mumbai
item.description: International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said trade talks between Canada and India advanced over the past week as he led a major trade mission to New Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said trade talks between Canada and India advanced over the past week as he led a major trade mission to New Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai. A statement from his office said the mission included representatives from nearly 300 Canadian businesses and exporters, and resulted in 34 commercial agreements worth almost $300 million. It said the agreements spanned multiple sectors, including aerospace, clean technology and energy transitions, information and communications technologies, infrastructure, life sciences and tourism. Sidhu’s office also said the minister met with Indian Industry Minister Piyush Goyal in both New Delhi and Mumbai to push forward trade talks. Canada and India are looking to conclude negotiations on a new Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement by the end of the year. The ministers have now met 10 times since May 2025. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi formally launched trade negotiations almost a year ago on the sidelines of the G20 leaders’ summit in South Africa. Carney confirmed on Thursday Modi will visit Toronto and Ottawa on Dec. 11 and 12, just ahead of this year’s G20 summit in Miami. The Liberals have set out to double non-U.S. exports over the next decade and have also set a goal of doubling two-way trade with India to $70 billion annually by 2030. In 2025, two-way goods and services trade between Canada and India amounted to $30.4 billion. In May, Goyal said Carney’s visit to his country paved the way for a complete overhaul of the Canada-India relationship. Canada and India have been in trade talks since 2010. But those talks were shut down in 2023 after the federal government accused New Delhi of playing a role in the assassination of a Canadian Sikh activist in Surrey, B.C. Carney, who made resetting relations with India a priority after he became prime minister in 2025, visited Mumbai and New Delhi in March. It was the first visit there by a Canadian prime minister in eight years. That trip concluded with a meeting with Modi and the signing of a series of agreements — including a $2.6-billion deal to supply India with about 22 million pounds of uranium for energy generation and 10 commercial agreements worth more than $5.5 billion. “From energy and critical minerals to aerospace, Canadian companies have built valuable connections that will strengthen our long-term partnership with one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies,” Sidhu said in a statement. “Canada is ready to be the reliable partner India needs, and the opportunities secured on this mission will deliver lasting benefits for our workers and businesses.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026 Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

item.title: U.S. markets weighed down by extended sell-off in the tech sector
item.description: The S&P 500 was down 1.1 per cent as of 2:01 p.m. Eastern time and on track for a weekly loss. The benchmark index is pulling back from the all-time high it set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — A broad sell-off in technology companies pulled stocks lower on Wall Street Friday, capping off the market’s worst week since late June. The S&P 500 fell 1.1 per cent. Its roughly 2 per cent drop for the week wiped out its gains from last week, when it set an all-time high. The Nasdaq composite, which is heavily weighted with technology stocks, sank 2.1 per cent and posted its first weekly loss in five weeks and its worst since June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average held up better, closing 0.3 per cent lower. Slightly more than half of the stocks in the S&P 500 fell, but all but seven of the 75 stocks in the index’s tech sector closed lower. Among the biggest decliners were chip companies, reflecting mounting worries about how long the frenzy over the AI buildout will last. Micron Technology fell 5.6 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6 per cent, Broadcom lost 4.5 per cent and Intel gave up 5.8 per cent. Among the other tech companies that finished in the red were Meta, which fell 3.7 per cent, and Google parent Alphabet, which dropped 2.5 per cent. It’s been a choppy week for chipmakers and other big tech stocks central to the artificial intelligence industry. Investors are now worried that the companies, which have relied on debt markets to finance an investment spree into their technology, may not be able to keep borrowing and spending as heavily with yields in bond markets worldwide recently climbing to their highest levels in years. Netflix’s stock fell 2.9 per cent a day after the company announced that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. The news comes just days after Netflix said that it plans to lay off about 6 per cent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions. Energy stocks held up better than most. Exxon rose 2.5 per cent and Chevron added 2.6 per cent. European and Asian markets closed higher. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.09 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. Yields are down despite reports this week showing that inflation at the consumer and wholesale level rose more in the U.S. than economists expected. The reports could persuade the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate before the end of this year. The central bank increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9 per cent in September, its first increase in three years. Wall Street traders expect the Fed will keep its short-term rate unchanged at its policy meeting this month, but the odds of a rate increase at the December meeting have jumped to 74.3 per cent from 50.2 per cent a month ago, according to data from the CME Group. On Friday, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no fresh signals about potential interest rate policy moves by the Fed while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. Elsewhere in the market, shares in Tesla fell 2.1 per cent after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new model of its Roadster sports car that can thrust itself up in the air. Alcoa rose 2.5 per cent and The Travelers Cos. gained 1.5 per cent after the companies reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street forecasts. Expectations are high for growth in profits from all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. That’s what’s allowed U.S. stocks to set records despite high inflation and the many other worries weighing on Wall Street. All told, the S&P 500 fell 84.62 points to 7,659.44. The Dow dropped 175.28 points to 52,002.41, and the Nasdaq declined 572.99 points to close at 26,140.03. In energy markets, oil prices remained elevated as the global oil supply continues to be under pressure without a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 3.7 per cent to settle at US$109.86 per barrel. That is up from around US$72 a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Brent climbed into triple digits last month, the first time since July. The national average for gasoline is at US$4.33 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. While that’s lower than the US$4.37 a gallon that it averaged last month, it’s sharply higher than the US$3.06 a gallon from a year ago. Oil remains well-supported as uncertainties surrounding the situation in the Middle East and concerns over oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz had the market “pricing in a significant risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary Friday. --- Alex Veiga, The Associated Press

item.title: U.S. fiscal 2026 budget deficit rises to US$1.99 trillion, largest in 5 years
item.description: The U.S. budget deficit rose by US$217 billion to $1.99 trillion in the 2026 fiscal year, fuelled in part by tariff refunds and record spending to service the nation’s more-than $40 trillion in debt, ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: The U.S. budget deficit rose by US$217 billion to $1.99 trillion in the 2026 fiscal year, fuelled in part by tariff refunds and record spending to service the nation’s more-than $40 trillion in debt, marking the largest budget shortfall in five years, Treasury Department figures reported on Friday showed. The results for the year ended September 30, the first full budget year of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term, compared to a $1.78 trillion deficit in fiscal 2025. It was the largest shortfall since fiscal 2021’s $2.77 trillion budget gap, then fueled by COVID-19 pandemic relief spending, and is the third- largest annual deficit ever. Total receipts for fiscal 2026 were a record $5.40 trillion, up $169 billion, or three per cent, from the $5.24 trillion in fiscal 2025. Fiscal 2026 outlays also were a record at $7.40 trillion, up $386 billion, or six per cent, from the $7.01 trillion in the prior fiscal year. Debt-service outlays totaled a record $1.36 trillion, climbing by $144 billion, or 12 per cent, a spending category now eclipsed only by Social Security and the combined outlays for Medicare and Medicaid. Total U.S. debt breached the $40 trillion milestone about two months ago. Another driver of the widening shortfall was a $22 billion drop in net tariff receipts following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling this year negating a large portion of the tariffs Trump had imposed during his first year in office. That triggered $145 billion of tariff refunds over this year, resulting in an 11 per cent decline in net tariff income to about $173 billion. A U.S. Treasury official said the department calculated an estimated deficit-to-GDP ratio of 6.2 per cent for fiscal 2026, but declined to say what GDP estimate was used. This figure compares to an actual 5.8 per cent deficit-to-GDP ratio for fiscal 2025. For the 2026 fiscal year’s final month of September, the Treasury reported a deficit of $27 billion versus a $198 billion surplus a year earlier. (Reporting by Dan Burns; Editing by Andrea Ricci)
